sm: Ben Shapiro opens with the shock news that Jensen Huang has been restored as CEO of Nvidia, the world's largest company, after his scandal-ridden exit. Nvidia stock jumped more than thirty percent and the market gained about three trillion dollars. President Trump applauded the board's decision, saying the country needs Huang's leadership. Shapiro says the restoration matters on three levels: business, economic and political, and he calls the political level potentially disastrous for the tech industry and the Republican Party. He notes that Nvidia makes up roughly six to eight percent of the S&P 500 and, per Goldman Sachs, a quarter of market growth.

On the business level, Shapiro explains that Huang is the leading advocate of open models in AI, in conflict with Dario Amodei, who backs closed models. He uses a cake analogy: open source publishes the recipe and sells the ingredients, while closed source keeps the recipe secret and sells the cake. Open models, he says, mean competition, innovation, lower prices and security through scrutiny, and Huang also wants to sell chips to China to make it dependent on American technology. Amodei argues for safety, regulation and the economics of funding expensive models. Shapiro sides with Huang, though he notes Anthropic is currently ahead in the AI race.

Shapiro turns to the economic case, noting the market tanked when Huang stepped down. He describes Nvidia's circular financing, in which it lends to or takes equity in customers such as SpaceX, Intel and CoreWeave, who then buy its chips and server space. He compares it to the biggest car dealership in history, helping customers finance purchases. Nvidia's commitments grew by about 140 billion dollars last quarter, and he quotes the Wall Street Journal and BBC on fears of an AI bubble and of Nvidia being too big to fail. Scott Bessent blames the selloff partly on Democrats' stance on AI buildout and on the Federal Reserve.

Then Shapiro gets to the political problem. The recent election's top issue was corruption, and AI data centers did badly. He lays out the story Democrats will tell: a top tech CEO had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the Commerce Department carved exceptions letting chips flow toward China, and the White House then intervened to reinstate him. He says he cannot tell whether the evidence is there, but the narrative of corruption, going soft on China, and too big to fail is potent. He warns Republicans would take the blame if Democrats crater the economy.

Shapiro cites a New York Times report that the woman at the center of the scandal, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security for more than a year while in a relationship with Huang. Her company, Megaspeed, bought large quantities of advanced Nvidia chips, some suspected of being smuggled to China. He stresses Huang left over chip diversion suspicions, not the affair. Jay Clayton says China did get top chips, and Senator John Kennedy says he wants to question Howard Lutnik and Scott Bessent. Bessent says Treasury, the trade representative and State wanted Megaspeed on the entity list, but Commerce held the pen.

He then lists other suspicions: Lutnik's Epstein island visit followed by a 25 million dollar donation to Trump's library, Nvidia's pledge to the White House ballroom, and Trump's investment accounts trading Nvidia stock over a hundred times. He adds government equity stakes tied to Trump allies and the meme coin dinner. Trump posted that he hoped Nvidia would rehire Huang, reportedly dialed into the board meeting, and his aide said he was totally involved. Nvidia's statement says the board got input from senior government levels and that its investigation was not finished. Shapiro says the White House now owns all of it.

Shapiro reads Trump's Truth Social statement calling Huang a great patriot and national treasure, and says he cannot name another case of a president directly intervening to restore a private company's ousted CEO. The Attorney General says the government has no evidence of unlawful contact by Huang. Shapiro responds that this raises the question of why shipments were lawful in the first place. He plays Trump on CNBC downplaying the China angle and saying the sex scandal drew attention. Shapiro insists the scandal was never about sex, but about corruption, chip access for China and ties to the White House.

He then discusses the coming tech backlash. He cites Alex Wang's claim that AI solved the Riemann hypothesis with a 250,000 page proof, and Wang's warning about recursive self-improvement and superintelligence. Shapiro says he is more sanguine about AI, but cites an FBI warning about AI-driven hacking and predictions of frequent cyber disruptions in 2027. His forecast: a short-term boom, then investigations and turmoil, and long-term chaos for Republicans. If Democrats win power, he fears open borders, nationalized health care and weakness on defense, and he warns about the intertwining of politics and business.

Shapiro says the public likes policy ideas but dislikes how enforcement looks, citing police work and immigration. He discusses viral video from Seattle airport where ICE arrested a father with a deportation order and his daughter, who threw hot coffee at officers. Their lawyer says they were headed to a baptism and she had applied to adjust her status through marriage to a citizen. Shapiro argues overstaying a visa is a crime and the left abstracts to abolishing ICE. He plays activists chanting and Washington Governor Bob Ferguson calling for abolition, and notes rising homelessness in King County.

He moves to a Polish influencer upset when ships would not pick up migrants, and to Denmark's prime minister saying she wants a strong majority culture and a Christian nation. He says Europe is reacting and Democrats would push open borders. He then turns to Medicare for All, noting Abdul El-Sayed's backing of Bernie Sanders's bill and the Trumpcare branding that Trump re-posted. Shapiro argues it would eliminate private insurance and compares Swiss, Singaporean and British models.

He plays Peggy Flanagan saying she would accept the Trumpcare label, and Senator John Kennedy saying the name does not matter and that the government cannot even deliver the mail. Shapiro says health care involves a tradeoff among universality, quality and affordability, where you can have only two. He says Switzerland's model does not scale to a country of 340 million people. He closes by saying Democrats will keep pushing it because national debt lets them confiscate more wealth.
